meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Who decided Owen gets a zero, and when was he asked about it?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.
Pretty conclusive. Turnitin's own guide says its score should never be the sole basis for punishing a student, and I have it printed in my bag. What else do you have, Hale?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. So what do you actually have?

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.
11:31, 11:52, 11:58, I'm writing that down. He told me he wrote it over the weekend, so he could have drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in.

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
Scroll to the end of the scene. A seventeen-year-old misquoting Shakespeare isn't proof of anything, Hale.
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
Hand me the outline. Students change their argument between an outline and a final draft; that's the point of drafting.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.

Five minutes after class, and a tired seventeen-year-old says "like, being stuck"; that's your impression, not a document. A forty-minute timed piece in September tells me nothing about a weekend essay. Print me the version history and that outline, and tell me what you're proposing.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
Under 4.4, then: in writing tonight, private, nothing on his record, and the rewrite marked well before his December 1 deadline. He'll do it to put this behind him, not because he did anything wrong.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.
Thursday, November 12, after school. Who else has seen this, and is anything on his record right now?
Do we have an agreement?
Not until you answer me. Is anything on his record right now?
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL
Hale,

You agreed today to a private, supervised rewrite under procedure 4.4 on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing placed on Owen's record. I still require confirmation of whether anything is on his record right now, and who else has seen this matter. I expect that agreement in writing tonight, and the mark entered before December 1.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF
Where she ended: She reached her last position and agreed to a private supervised rewrite on Thursday after school with nothing on his record; she still wants to know whether anything is on his record right now and who else has seen this, and that rewrite under procedure 4.4 is the fair outcome.
What moved her: You laid out dated evidence she could check and then offered the private rewrite under 4.4 in writing, which met her one non-negotiable about his record.
What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it conclusive, which handed her the strongest argument she had prepared.
What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked; your version history put the writing late on the night before the essay was due, very close to that kind of night, though it proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.
Try next time: When she asked whether anything was on his record right now, answer that directly instead of asking whether you had an agreement.
